How an operating system works

Right now your computer is running a browser, an editor, a terminal and a long list of programs you never started. Each of them behaves as if the machine were its own: it computes when it likes, keeps its data where it likes and reads its files without asking who else is about. Yet the machine has only a handful of CPU cores, one memory and one disk. This page is about what makes this work: the operating system, and the one program at its heart.

It picks up where How a CPU works stops. If instructions, registers, the program counter and the clock's tick are new to you, start there.

Below is a small machine with one CPU and three programs. sum adds up a list of eight numbers that it reads from a tape. primes counts the prime numbers below 100. editor shows what somebody types. Change the speed with the slider, pause it and step one tick at a time (a tick is one beat of the machine's clock, and this machine carries out one instruction per tick), or press the button to type a key yourself:

All three make progress: letters appear, the total grows, the count of primes climbs. But the strip along the bottom, which records who had the CPU on each tick, never shows two at once. The CPU does one instruction of sum, or of primes, or of the editor, and they take turns so quickly that each seems to run without a break.

Some ticks belong to none of the three. They are drawn in violet, and they fall wherever a program hands over to another or a device reports in. A fourth program is at work in them, which the figure labels "kernel". It owns the machine and lends it to the others a few ticks at a time, and it alone touches the devices, the tape and the keyboard. If you press no keys, then after 133 ticks sum has its total, 31, primes has counted 25 primes, and the fourth program has taken 26 ticks for itself.

We are going to build that fourth program. We start in the early 1950s with a machine that has none, and add its parts in the order in which people were forced to invent them. The machine and the three programs stay the same all the way.

Before any of that, let's put one program on the machine, alone.

1. One program, one machine

It is the early 1950s, and there is no operating system because nobody has thought of one. There is a machine, and there is you, with a program. The machine is the one the CPU page ended up with: a memory of 256 numbered cells and a CPU with four registers and a program counter. I have made one simplification for this page: it carries out exactly one instruction on every tick. The program in its memory is primes:

The strip under the machine is how this page keeps score. Every tick adds one square to it, in the colour of whoever had the CPU on that tick. Here all 80 squares are orange, because primes computes on every tick until it has its answer, 25. The meter beside the strip shows the busy share: the share of the ticks on which the CPU did a program's own work. For this program, alone on this machine, it is 100%.

A device is two cells

primes needs nothing from outside. sum does. Its list, the numbers 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2 and 6 from the CPU page, is on a reel of magnetic tape. A tape drive, a keyboard, a printer: anything that is neither the CPU nor memory is a device, and moving numbers to and from devices is called input and output, or I/O.

A device shows the CPU a couple of cells that look like memory but are wired to the device instead. The tape has two. Its status cell reads 0 while the tape is moving and 1 when a number is ready. Its data cell then holds the number. Step through sum fetching its first number:

The tape needs 8 ticks to bring a number under its reading head. The program has no way to learn that the number has arrived except by looking. So it looks at the status cell, finds a 0, and looks again: one instruction, carried out over and over. Seven looks find nothing and the eighth finds the number, eight ticks that accomplish nothing.

Only then come two ticks of real work: one instruction adds the number to the total, and one counts down the numbers still to come. Taking the number out of the data cell also sets the tape moving towards the next one. (For this page I have given our machine two convenient instructions that the CPU page did not have: one that looks at a cell and goes round again while it holds 0, and one that counts down and branches.)

Here is the whole list. The first slider changes how many ticks the tape needs for each number:

The run takes 80 ticks, and sum works in 16 of them. The other 64 go on asking the tape whether it is ready, so the busy share is 20%. With a tape so quick that the first look finds the number it would be 67%, and with a slower tape it sinks towards nothing. The program is not badly written. The machine is simply waiting for its tape.

How slow is slow

Our tape takes four times as long as the work between two reads. Real devices are far worse. The next figure puts one instruction and several device events on one scale of time, on which each step to the right is ten times longer than the one before. A millisecond (ms) is a thousandth of a second, a microsecond (µs) a millionth and a nanosecond (ns) a thousand-millionth. Choose the machine, and switch on the human scale:

An IBM 704 of 1955 could do up to 12,000 floating-point additions a second, and its card reader passed one card in 0.4 seconds: 4,800 such additions for every card. Stretch time until one addition takes a second, and a card takes 80 minutes. Since then CPUs have gained much more than devices have. Take a round thousand million instructions a second for a CPU of today. On the human scale the arm of a hard disk needs about four months to reach its place, and a single character typed at ten a second arrives after three years.

The open shop

The slowest device of all was the programmer. A program was a deck of punched cards. You put your name on a list, and when your turn came the machine was yours.

Robert Patrick, who programmed an IBM 701 in 1954, wrote down what followed. You checked the plugboards, the panels of plugged wires that set up the card reader, the printer and the card punch. You hung a tape, set the switches on the console, put your deck in the reader and pressed Load. For a deck of 300 cards, about five minutes passed before the first instruction ran. A jammed card made it ten. The sliders set the minutes of setup and of running, and the button jams a card:

With five minutes of setup for three of running, the machine computes for little more than a third of the hour. "Usually the machine spent more time idle than computing," Patrick wrote. By Patrick's figure a 701 was rented for about 23,750 dollars a month, which comes to about 137 dollars for each hour of a working week, and an hour of standing idle cost the same as an hour of computing.

About three of those five minutes went on loading the deck. Patrick cut that part to ten seconds, by keeping to standard plugboards and loading from tape. With setup down to a little over two minutes the machine computes for more than half the hour. The lessons he drew went further: standard setups, programs kept on tape, and the programmer out of the machine room.

2. A program that runs programs

In 1955 the IBM 704 arrived, more than twice as fast as the 701 and fitted with the same card reader, printer and punch. The faster the CPU, the larger the share of every hour that went on people shuffling cards. "We recognized we had to change our mode of operation," wrote Patrick, by then working on a 704 for General Motors.

The change was to keep one small program in memory for good, whose only work is to load the next program. Everybody's decks are copied onto one tape beforehand, card after card, and each deck is headed by one extra card that says "a new job starts here". A program handed in like this, with its cards, is a job, and the small program that stays in memory is the monitor (in full, the resident monitor). Step through two jobs:

The monitor sits in the lowest cells of memory. It reads a job card, copies sum into the cells above itself and jumps there. From then on the monitor is not running at all. It runs again only when the last instruction of sum jumps back to cell 0, and then it loads primes over the top of sum. Notice what hands the CPU back: the job's own last instruction. We will return to that.

The system that General Motors and North American Aviation built this way for their 704s was in use by 1957, and about twenty 704 sites ran it. Most of it was two programs that translated the decks before the jobs ran and the results afterwards. The part that stayed in memory while the jobs ran was 300 of the machine's 8,192 words, a word being that machine's cell.

Running jobs one behind another from a tape is called batch processing. Here are six jobs of a minute each, done both ways:

By hand, with five minutes of setup before each job, the six take 36 minutes. Loaded by the monitor they take 6. Patrick remembered the time lost between jobs falling "from minutes to milliseconds", and about sixty test jobs an hour going through where people had booked the machine in blocks of six minutes.

The programmers paid for it. You no longer stood at the console. You handed in a deck and came back later for the printout. That could take hours, and every mistake in the deck cost the whole wait again.

One copy of the tape routine

The monitor brought a second gain. In the open shop every deck carried its own routines for input and output and for converting numbers, picked by each programmer from a shelf. But the monitor is always in memory, so those routines can live in it, once. Flip the switch, and then repair the mistake in the routine:

With the switch off there are three copies of the tape routine, and its mistake has to be repaired three times, once in each deck. With it on, every job shrinks to its own instructions and a jump to a fixed address in the monitor, and one repair serves everybody. This is the humblest thing an operating system is, and it has never stopped being it: a set of routines that every program uses and nobody has to bring.

The score

Back to our machine. Its tape now holds two jobs, sum and primes. Choose which goes first:

The two jobs take 160 ticks, and in 96 of them the CPU does a job's own work: a busy share of 60%. (I am not counting the few ticks the monitor needs to load each job.) That is better than 20% only because primes brought 80 ticks of solid work with it. The 64 ticks that sum spends asking the tape are exactly where they were. The order decides only who waits: put primes first, and the total of sum arrives at tick 160 instead of 80.

Three ways to wreck it

The monitor is a program like any other. It lies in the same memory as the jobs and is run by the same CPU, which treats its instructions no differently from theirs. Pick what is wrong with the job in the middle of this tape. It comes after sum, so give it a few seconds, or raise the speed:

One wrong address is enough. The job stores a number into a cell of the monitor, and when it later jumps back, the monitor carries out garbage and the machine stops, with primes still on the tape.

Patrick's 704 "had no limit registers or any other way to partition off and protect the operating system", and he recalled programs that "ran away during execution and destroyed the operating system in low core". ("Core" was the word for memory, and the monitor lay at its low end. Limit registers are a way of fencing memory off. We will build them in section 8, under the name of bound registers.)

A job that loops for ever never jumps back at all, and only a person at the console can end it. A job that reads one card too many is reading the same tape as the monitor, and could swallow the card that announces the next job.

The whole arrangement rests on good manners. "Our application programmers were company-loyal and not mischievous," Patrick wrote. To protect the monitor from a program that is mistaken, or mischievous, the machine itself has to change.

3. Two modes and one door

Two of the three wrecks were a job doing something that only the monitor should do: storing into the monitor's cells, and working the tape itself. A job should be unable to do either, or to halt the machine. The monitor has to be able to do all three, on the same CPU.

So the CPU must know which of the two it is running, and one bit is enough to tell it. Call it the mode bit. It has two settings: user mode, in which jobs run, and kernel mode, for the monitor. The monitor gets a new name to go with it, which it keeps for the rest of the page: the kernel.

One register goes with the bit, the boundary, which holds the number of the first cell a job may touch. The cells of the devices count as the kernel's too. (I have also changed the tape a little: from here on it starts moving only when a 1 is stored in its first cell, so that there is something to forbid.) Choose the mode and an instruction to try:

In user mode the addition goes through as always. The store into cell 5, the store that starts the tape and the halt are refused: the CPU does not carry them out, and enters the kernel instead (how, we will see under the next heading). In kernel mode all four are carried out, the halt included. An instruction that works only in kernel mode is a privileged instruction. Changing the mode bit or the boundary is privileged too, of course.

"Operating system" will from here on mean the kernel together with the programs that are shipped with it.

Nobody can say which machine had such a bit first. The Atlas computer at Manchester had one in 1962. MIT's IBM 7094, which had none as it left the factory, got one as a special order in 1963. With IBM's System/360, announced in April 1964, it became standard equipment: one bit of that machine's status word says "problem state" or "supervisor state", and every instruction that works a device is privileged.

The door

A job can now not read the tape at all. It has to ask the kernel to do it, and the asking has to switch the CPU into kernel mode without letting the job run a single instruction of its own there. One new instruction does this, the trap instruction. Step through it:

The trap does three things in one tick. It saves the program counter, so that the program can be resumed. It sets the mode bit to kernel. And it loads the program counter from a cell that only the kernel can write. So a program can get into kernel mode whenever it likes, but it arrives at a place the kernel chose, inside the kernel's own code. The last step shows the program trying to change that cell: it lies below the boundary, and the store is refused.

A refused instruction takes the same route. The CPU saves the program counter, switches to kernel mode and lands at another address of the kernel's choosing, where the kernel decides what to do about the offender.

Everything on the rest of this page stands on this one door.

Asking the kernel

A request made through the trap is a system call. The program says what it is asking for by putting a number in a register before it traps. Here is sum asking for its next number:

sum puts 0, which means "read", in r0 and traps. The kernel looks up 0 in its own table of system calls, works the tape itself (the same loop of asking as before, now in kernel mode), leaves the number in r1 and returns to the instruction after the trap. sum never touches the tape, and no longer contains a single instruction that could.

On our machine an entry into the kernel costs one tick, so that you can see it: a number now takes 11 ticks where it took 10. Keep in mind that this is a toy's figure, and that our programs call the kernel after every two ticks of work, far more often than real ones do. We will get to real figures shortly.

The same thing on Linux

Here is one line of C on a present-day PC running Linux, write(1, "hi\n", 3), which sends three bytes to the terminal. Step through what the machine does with it:

The parts are the ones you have just met, under other names. The number of the system call goes in the register rax: 1 means write, and 0 means read, which is where our toy table got its numbers. The three arguments go in rdi, rsi and rdx.

The instruction syscall is the trap: it keeps the address of the next instruction in rcx, switches to kernel mode and jumps to an address that the kernel put into a special register when it started. The kernel saves the program's registers and sees from the 1 in rax that this is a write. It looks up the call's first argument, which is also a 1 and here stands for the terminal (sections 12 and 14 explain how), hands over the bytes, puts 3 in rax to say how many it wrote, and goes back with sysret.

Linux offers nearly 400 system calls on such a machine. Whatever a program does beyond computing in its own memory, it does through one of them.

The faulty jobs again

Here are the three jobs that wrecked the batch in the last section, on a machine with a mode bit and a boundary. As before, the bad job runs after sum:

The store into the kernel's cells is refused, the kernel is entered, and it throws the job out and loads the next: primes runs and answers 25. Linux does the same to a program that tries a privileged instruction, with a message whose odd wording, "Segmentation fault", we will come back to. The job that reads past its cards cannot work the tape any more. It has to ask the kernel for its next card, and the kernel, which read the job cards, knows where each job's cards end.

The endless loop is another matter. It is refused nothing, because it asks for nothing. It still holds the machine. Remember it: we will need one more piece of hardware to deal with it.

The price of the door

Now the real figures. The bars compare a function call, a system call and a third thing that I will come to, and the slider cuts a file of 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) into reads of the size you choose:

In one measurement made in 2018, calling a function took 1.77 ns and a trivial system call about 235 ns: some 130 times longer. A program that reads its megabyte one byte at a time spends 246 ms on the crossings alone. Reading 4,096 bytes at a time takes 256 calls and 60 µs. That is why well-written programs ask for a lot at once and hand it out to themselves in small pieces.

The middle bar shows the other remedy, which is not to cross at all. Programs ask the time so often that Linux keeps the clock in a piece of memory every program is allowed to read, and no trap is needed.

And the score? With two modes sum needs 88 ticks and the two jobs 168, so the busy share has gone down a little, from 60% to 57%. Safety has a price. Worse, the kernel has inherited the silliest job on the machine: it now stands in a loop asking the tape whether it is ready.

4. The device speaks first

Asking a device over and over whether it is ready has a name, polling, and it puts whoever does it in a bind. To see the bind, let a program do useful work and look at the keyboard only now and then. The slider sets how many ticks of work pass between two looks:

Look after every 4 ticks of work, and a fifth of the machine's time goes on questions that are nearly always answered "nothing yet". Look after every 40, and hardly a tick is wasted, but a key lies unnoticed for about 20 ticks. No setting is right. Polling is wasteful or slow, and usually some of both.

The way out is to turn the conversation round and let the device speak first. Give it a wire into the CPU, which it raises when it has something. And have the CPU glance at the wire between one instruction and the next, which costs it nothing. Step through a keypress arriving while primes is running:

If the wire is up, the CPU does just what the trap instruction made it do: it saves the program counter, switches to kernel mode and takes the next address from a place the kernel prepared. This is an interrupt, and the piece of the kernel that then runs is an interrupt handler. Here the handler takes the key out of the keyboard's data cell, which lowers the wire, and returns. primes goes on with its very next instruction and never knows it was away.

Machines began to get such a wire in the middle of the 1950s. Which was first is still argued about.

One table

The CPU now has three reasons to enter the kernel, and it treats them alike. Press the buttons to cause each:

A system call, an interrupt from a device, and an instruction the CPU refuses to carry out all go through one table of addresses, the interrupt table, which the kernel fills in when it starts. A refused instruction is called a fault (or an exception): dividing by zero is one, and so is a privileged instruction in user mode.

The three differ in two things only. One is who causes the entry: the program with its trap, a device, or the CPU itself. The other is what follows. After a system call or a device's interrupt the program carries on at its next instruction. After a fault like these two the kernel normally ends the program.

From here on I will say that the CPU enters the kernel, whichever of the three it was. On a PC running Linux the table has 256 rows: dividing by zero is row 0, a refused instruction row 13, and devices use the rows from 32 up. (The syscall instruction of the last section is a later shortcut, with an entry address of its own.)

Sum, interrupted

Now the tape gets its wire. Here is sum on such a machine:

For each number there is one kernel tick for the call. The kernel starts the tape and then has nothing to do. It carries out the halt instruction, which on a machine with interrupts stops the CPU only until the next one arrives, and the CPU stands idle for 8 ticks. The tape raises its wire, the handler takes one more kernel tick to fetch the number, and sum does its two ticks of work. Nobody asks anybody anything.

Too many interrupts

Interrupts are a bargain while events are as rare as our tape's, and they have a limit of their own. Here the device is a network card, which receives messages from other machines in small pieces called packets and raises its wire for each one. The slider sets how many arrive:

At 20 packets in every 100 ticks all is well. Taking a packet from the card is only the beginning: the kernel then has to work out which program the packet is for and hand it over, and it does that when no interrupt is waiting. At 90 packets an interrupt is nearly always waiting. The kernel hardly ever gets round to finishing a packet, so fewer get through than at a lower rate, and primes stops altogether.

This was reported for a real router in 1996: the packets it forwarded peaked at 4,700 a second and then fell as more arrived, because, as the authors put it, "the system spends all its time processing interrupts".

The cure is to go back to asking, at the right moment. After the first interrupt the kernel switches the card's interrupts off and collects packets a batch at a time, with other work in between. What the card cannot hold meanwhile, the card throws away, at no cost to the CPU. Linux's network code works like this. For a device that answers within microseconds, plain polling can even win outright: one fast storage device completed a read in 4.4 µs when polled and 7.6 µs through an interrupt.

The score

Back to our tape. We now have three ways of running the same two jobs. Here they are on one scale:

160 ticks, then 168, then 176. The 64 ticks of waiting have changed hands twice: first the program asked them away, then the kernel did, and now they are simply left empty. The busy share has gone from 60% to 57% to 55%. Each step made the machine safer or quieter, and none of them touched the waiting itself. Still, something has changed. During those 64 ticks the CPU is now free, and it is free because nothing has thought to use it.

5. Two programs in memory

While sum waits for the tape, the CPU stands idle, and further along the same tape primes is waiting for that very CPU. The remedy needs only a memory large enough to hold several programs at once: when one of them has to wait, the CPU runs another. How much could that gain? Suppose every program waits 80% of the time, as sum does, and put more and more of them in memory:

The CPU is idle only when all the programs happen to be waiting at the same moment. With one program it is busy 20% of the time. With two, 36%. With five, 67%, and with ten, 89%. The curve is 1 − 0.8ⁿ for n programs. It is a model and not a measurement: it assumes that the programs wait independently of one another and that going from one to the next costs nothing. But it shows where the idle ticks can go. For programs that wait half the time, three are enough to keep the CPU busy 88% of the time.

The switch

To run primes in the middle of sum, the kernel has to stop sum in such a way that it can go on later as if nothing had happened. Everything sum is in the middle of is held in the registers and the program counter. Step through what the kernel does with them:

sum makes its call for the next number. The kernel starts the tape. Then it copies the four registers and the saved program counter into a row of a table it keeps, copies another row of the table into the CPU, and returns. The CPU is now running primes, at exactly the instruction where primes last stopped. This is a context switch. (A real kernel saves in two stages, most registers on entering the kernel and the rest at the switch itself, but the effect is the same.)

A program that is being run like this, with a row of its own in the kernel's table, is called a process, and the table is the process table. From here on I will keep the two words apart: a program is a set of instructions, and a process is a program that is running, together with everything the kernel keeps about it. One program can be several processes at once, and soon we will run primes twice.

Three states

The table also records, for each process, what it is waiting for. Press the buttons and watch the three processes move:

A process is running when it has the CPU, ready when it could use the CPU but does not have it, and blocked when it is waiting for a device and the CPU would be no use to it. Only four moves exist. The kernel picks a ready process and it runs. A running process asks for something slow and is blocked. A device finishes, and the process blocked on it becomes ready. And a running process goes back to being ready when the kernel gives the CPU to another.

There is no move from blocked straight to running: a process woken by its device always passes through the queue of ready ones. On our machine it goes to the head of that queue and gets the CPU at once, and the process it interrupted is next in line behind it.

The score

Here are sum and primes one at a time, as in the last section, and below them the two together in memory:

During every one of the eight waits of sum, primes computes. Both are finished after 112 ticks where they took 176, the CPU is never idle, and the busy share has jumped from 55% to 86%. The 16 ticks that remain are the kernel's: eight calls and eight interrupts.

Machines began to work like this around 1960. The practice was called multiprogramming, and the Atlas computer of about 1962 and IBM's OS/360 a few years later were built on it.

What a switch costs

On our machine the kernel took 16 of those 112 ticks. On a real machine its share is far smaller, because a real program does much more than two instructions of work between one call and the next. But a real switch has a cost that our ticks do not show. The slider sets how much data each of two processes is working on:

The switch itself took about 6 µs on a PC of 1996, 3.8 µs in 2007 and between 1.2 and 1.5 µs in 2018. But the process switched to finds the CPU's cache full of the other process's data, and its first accesses miss. In the 2007 measurement a switch cost 4 to 9 µs all told while the data of both processes fitted in the cache together, and up to about 1,500 µs when it did not. The hidden price can be hundreds of times the visible one.

The hog

Now put everything in memory at once: the editor, sum, primes, and a second copy of primes as a process of its own, drawn in a lighter orange:

The editor and sum do well. Each waits for a device, gets the CPU the moment the device answers, and is soon waiting again. The first copy of primes never asks for anything, and so, between those short visits, nothing ever takes the CPU away from it. The second copy stays ready for 129 ticks before it gets its first one, when the first copy has finished.

Let the first copy loop for ever, and the second stays ready for ever and never runs. This is the endless loop of section 3 again, and the same weakness. The kernel gets the CPU only when something enters it, and a program that neither asks for anything nor is interrupted on anyone's behalf can keep the CPU as long as it likes.

6. The clock that takes the CPU back

The kernel is entered by system calls, by faults and by the interrupts of devices. A program that computes quietly causes none of these. So add a device whose only purpose is to cause an interrupt: a timer. The kernel writes a number of ticks into it, and when that many ticks have passed, the timer raises its wire. Step through the two copies of primes on a machine that has one:

The kernel writes 4 into the timer and hands the CPU to the first copy. Four ticks later the timer interrupts, in the middle of a program that had asked for nothing, and the kernel is in charge again. It saves the first copy's registers, puts that process at the tail of the queue of ready processes, loads the second copy, winds the timer once more and returns.

To take the CPU from a running process like this is to preempt it, and the stretch a process may run before it is preempted is its time slice (also called a quantum). The endless loop is beaten at last. The timer interrupts it like any other program, and the kernel can end it, or just go on giving everybody else their turns.

How long a slice

The length of the slice is the kernel's to choose. Try it on the two copies of primes:

With a slice of 10 ticks the second copy waits 11 ticks for its first turn, and the kernel takes 14 of the run's 174 ticks: a busy share of 92%. With a slice of 40 the wait is 41 ticks and the busy share almost 99%. With a slice of 2 the wait is 3 ticks, and a third of all the ticks are the kernel's. Short slices give everybody a turn soon and charge for it.

The charge is exaggerated here, as before, because our slices are a handful of instructions long. A real switch takes a microsecond or two and a real slice lasts a few milliseconds, so the switches themselves cost about a twentieth of one percent.

This is also where the busy share stops being the interesting number. With enough processes in memory the CPU always has something to do. What matters from here on is how long each process, and the person behind it, has to wait.

Several machines out of one

Each of our four processes now has a small screen of its own for what it puts out: letters, running totals, or the primes it finds. Watch them slowly first, and then raise the speed:

At four ticks a second you can see the CPU serve one process at a time while the other three stand still. At a thousand ticks a second all four screens advance together, each as if it had a slower CPU to itself. Nothing has changed but the speed. People take a response that comes within about a tenth of a second as instant, so a machine that gets round all its processes faster than that seems to run them all at once. What you saw at the top of this page was no more than this.

What the timer protects against

Not every system took the CPU away from a running program. Some never did: a device's interrupt was dealt with and noted, but the program that had been running then carried on until it handed the CPU back of its own accord. Here are both kinds. On the left every program is well behaved at first, and hands over after a few ticks of work. The button makes primes loop without ever calling the kernel:

On the left one loop freezes everything. The keyboard's interrupt still arrives and the editor is marked ready, but the loop never hands over, so the editor never runs and no letter appears. On the right the timer keeps the others going. Programs written for early versions of Windows, and programs on the Macintosh until Mac OS X arrived in 2001, worked the left-hand way. One program that computed without handing over hung the whole system, and the remedy was to restart the machine.

Dozens of people, one machine

The timer made a new way of using computers possible. In a memo dated 1959, John McCarthy complained that an answer from MIT's computing centre took between 3 and 36 hours, and proposed aiming at "the order of 1 second": give every person a terminal, a keyboard with a printer or a screen that is wired to the machine, and let the machine go round them all, a slice each. MIT first showed such a system, CTSS, in November 1961, with three people at typewriters while a queue of batch jobs ran behind them. This is time sharing. The slider sets how many people share the machine:

With a slice of a fifth of a second and three people, a short command gets its turn within 0.4 seconds. With 25 people it waits up to 4.8 seconds, and a calculation that needs a minute of the CPU takes 25 minutes if everybody is calculating at once. The machine is no faster than before. It has stopped wasting the time of people, which had become the more expensive kind. By the summer of 1965 the system at Dartmouth College was serving 40 people at a time.

All of it rests on the kernel choosing, many times a second, who runs next. So far its answer has been "whoever is at the head of the queue", and that is not always a good answer.

7. Who runs next

The part of the kernel that picks the next process to run is the scheduler, and the queue of ready processes it picks from is the ready queue. The simplest rule is plain turns: every ready process gets one time slice and then goes to the tail. This is called round robin. Our machine has quietly been doing something a little cleverer since section 5: a process woken by its device goes to the head of the queue. Here is what that is worth. The top strip is pure round robin, the bottom one is ours:

The time from a keypress to the letter on the screen is the response. In pure round robin a woken editor waits for everybody ahead of it: with a slice of 10 it answers after 18 ticks, and with a slice of 40 after as many as 82. When the woken process goes first, the editor answers in 3 to 7 ticks whatever the slice, and sum is finished after 98 ticks where round robin, at a slice of 10, kept it going until tick 226. The machine, the slice and the work are the same in both strips.

Shortest first

Why does one small rule help so much? Because of how unequal the processes are. When the editor gets the CPU it needs it for 2 ticks and then waits again. primes needs it for 80. sum, like the editor, needs it for 2. Suppose all three are ready at the same moment, and choose who goes first:

With primes first, the three stretches of work end at ticks 80, 82 and 84, on average at 82. With primes last they end at 2, 4 and 84, on average at 30. primes lost 4 ticks and each of the others gained 80. The time from when a piece of work arrives to when it is finished is its turnaround. (Response is about how soon something happens at all, turnaround about when it is done.) For work that arrives together, running the shortest first gives the smallest average turnaround there can be.

The trouble is that the kernel cannot see how long a process is going to want the CPU.

Guessing from the past

What it can see is how the process behaved last time. The next scheduler keeps three queues, one above the other, and always serves the highest one that has anybody in it:

Every process starts on the top level. One that uses up a whole slice is moved down a level. One that blocks before its slice is over stays where it is. (Real schedulers of this kind add up the time a process has used at its level, so that it cannot stay on top by always stopping just short.)

After a few slices the editor and sum are on top, and both copies of primes are at the bottom, where the slices are longer: they run seldom, but for a good stretch when they do. Nobody told the kernel which process was which. They showed it. A level in such a scheme is a priority, and CTSS had a scheduler of this family in 1962.

Strict levels have a flaw, though. In the next figure short pieces of work keep arriving on the top level, as much as the slider says:

While short work takes half the CPU, primes gets most of the rest. Let short work fill the CPU, and the top level is never empty: primes gets no ticks at all. This is starvation. The usual cure is to lift every process back to the top at regular intervals, which guarantees even the lowest a slice now and then.

Counting instead

Levels, slices per level and lifts make a growing pile of rules. From 2007 Linux moved to a scheme with one number per process: a count of the CPU time the process has had. Each process also gets a weight, a number that says how large a share of the CPU it should have. The slider changes the weight of the second copy of primes:

The kernel always runs the process whose count is smallest. Two equal processes therefore share the CPU equally. Give one of them more weight, and its count grows more slowly for the same time on the CPU: at the setting Linux calls nice −5 (the lower the number, the greater the weight) its weight is about three times the ordinary one, and it gets 75% of the CPU to the other's 25%.

Meanwhile sum, which mostly waits, comes back each time with a small count and runs at once. "Woken goes first" falls out of the rule without being one. The kernel does not let a process save up its absence, though: a process that returns is placed only just below the smallest count.

Since 2023 Linux has used a successor of this scheduler, which keeps the count. Its slices are a few milliseconds long.

Several cores

The CPU page ended with several cores on one chip, and a scheduler has to fill all of them. Choose the number of cores, and switch the taking of work on and off:

Each core has a queue of its own, so that a process stays on the core whose cache holds its data. But the queues drift apart: without any exchange one core stands idle while processes wait in line at the other. So an idle core takes a process from the longest queue. The process that is moved pays for it, because it arrives to a cache that holds nothing of its own, and in this toy it works at half speed for its first few ticks. Balancing the queues against moving as little as possible is most of what a scheduler for many cores does.

So much for sharing out the CPU's ticks. The processes still share one memory, and nothing we have built stops one of them from storing a number into a cell that belongs to another.

8. A fence around each program

Here is the memory of our machine with all three programs loaded: the kernel in the lowest 64 cells, then sum, primes and the editor, and some free cells at the end. (For the next few sections, let sum keep its list in its own memory, as it did on the CPU page. Where the list comes from will matter again when we reach the disk.) The boundary of section 3 protects the kernel from all of them, and does nothing to protect them from one another. This version of sum has a mistake in it: it stores its total at the wrong address.

Watch where the total goes, and then look at the answer of primes:

The address is off by a little, and the store lands in cell 104, which happens to be where primes keeps its count. Nothing complains. primes finishes and reports 31 primes below 100, where there are 25. This is the worst kind of failure: it shows up in the wrong program, later, and without a word. Put a fence round sum, and the store is stopped at its edge. The kernel is entered, sum is ended, and primes answers 25.

Two registers

The fence consists of two registers in the CPU and a rule that the CPU applies to every address a program uses. Move the address with the slider:

The bound register (on some machines the limit register) holds the size of the program's memory, 32 cells for sum. The base register holds where that memory begins, cell 64. On every access the CPU checks that the address is below the bound, and then adds the base. So address 24, where sum keeps its list, becomes cell 88. Address 40 is not below 32, so it reaches no cell at all: it is a fault, and the kernel is entered.

Two terms belong here. The address a program uses is a virtual address, and the cell it finally lands in has a physical address. From now on a program never sees a physical address. The boundary register of section 3 can go: it was this fence in its crudest form, with only the kernel on the safe side. The idea of such a pair of registers dates from the late 1950s, and the CDC 6600 of 1964 guarded its programs with exactly this pair.

A fence for each

The fence is not part of the machine. It is part of the process. Step through a switch from sum to primes:

Base and bound are two more values in each row of the process table. The kernel saves and loads them with the other registers at every switch, and loading them is a privileged instruction. So each process runs inside a fence of its own and cannot move it: in the last step primes tries, and is refused.

Anywhere will do

The base register brings something beyond protection. Slide sum to another place in memory while it is running:

sum is written as if its memory began at cell 0, and it never learns otherwise. The kernel can load it wherever there is room. It can even move it between two of its instructions, by stopping it, copying its 32 cells and changing a single number in its row. The address 24 still leads to the list, and the total still comes to 31.

Holes

The scheme asks one thing of memory: every program must have one unbroken run of cells. Here four programs fill the memory. Let two of them end:

When B and D are gone, 80 cells are free. Program E needs 64 and cannot be loaded, because the free cells lie in two holes, of 32 and of 48. This is fragmentation. The kernel can close the gap by copying C's 64 cells down next to A, but a program has to stand still while it is moved, and after a few more arrivals and departures the holes are back.

The holes have one root: memory is being handed out in pieces of whatever size is asked for. And there is a second limit behind them. A program has to be in memory whole, so none can be larger than memory itself. The next section deals with the holes, and the one after it with the second limit.

9. Memory in pages

If pieces of different sizes leave holes, hand memory out in pieces of one size. Cut every program's addresses into pages of 16 cells and cut memory into frames of 16 cells, and any page can go into any frame. The first question is which page an address belongs to. Move the address:

It takes no arithmetic. Because 16 is a power of two, the lower four bits of an address are its place within the page, the offset, and the upper four bits are the number of the page. Address 24 is 0001 1000 in bits: page 1, offset 8.

A PC does the same with larger numbers. Most PCs use 48 of the 64 bits of an address, and its pages are 4,096 bytes long, so the lowest 12 bits are the offset and the 36 above them the page number. (A cell of memory holds one byte. From here on I give real sizes in bytes: a KiB is 1,024 bytes, a MiB 1,024 KiB, a GiB 1,024 MiB and a TiB 1,024 GiB. Where a source says MB or GB, I leave its figure as it stands.)

The table

In place of a base and a bound, each process now gets a table with one row for each of its pages, saying which frame holds it. This is its page table. Follow an address through it, and switch between the three processes:

The memory of sum is now three pages: its program, its list and, far up at page 15, its stack, the scratch space where a program keeps track of the functions it is in the middle of. They lie in frames 6, 9 and 4: scattered, and not even in order.

It makes no difference. The CPU splits address 24 into page 1 and offset 8, finds frame 9 in the row for page 1, and arrives at cell 152. For primes the same address 24 leads to cell 120. Each process has its own table, and therefore its own complete set of addresses from 0 to 255, which is called its address space.

A page with no row has no frame behind it. Address 100 is in page 6, which sum does not have, and the lookup stops there. One register in the CPU, the page-table register, says where the running process's table is, and the kernel changes it at every switch.

Now the test that the last section failed. On the left the programs get unbroken runs of cells, on the right pages:

With pages, the four pages of E go into any four free frames: two where B was and two where D was. Nothing is copied and nobody stands still. No hole can be too small any more, because every hole is exactly one frame.

Three bits per row

Each row of the table, called an entry, also carries a few bits of permission, which the CPU checks on every access. Choose a page and what to do to it:

The present bit says that the page has a frame at all. The writable bit says that it may be stored into: the page that holds the instructions of sum is not writable, so a program cannot overwrite its own instructions by accident. The user bit says that the page may be touched in user mode. The kernel's own pages appear in every process's table with that bit off, so the kernel finds its memory in place whenever it is entered and the process cannot reach it.

When an access breaks one of these rules, the instruction is not carried out: it is a fault, with a row of its own in the interrupt table. If the program had no business at that address, the kernel ends it, and the message is "Segmentation fault", a name left over from an older scheme in which a program's memory was divided into a few "segments" of different sizes.

If you write C you have met it through a null pointer: on real systems address 0 is deliberately left without a page, so that this mistake is caught at once. (Our toy puts a page there, to keep its numbers small.)

A table that is a tree

One line per page is easy when a process has 16 pages. A real one has rather more. Use the slider to change how much memory a process uses:

The 36 bits of page number on a PC make 2³⁶ pages. At 8 bytes an entry, a single table with a row for every page would take 512 GiB for each process, nearly all of it describing pages the process will never have.

So the table is built as a tree with four levels. Every table in it has 512 entries and fills exactly one frame, and an entry in an upper table says where a lower table is, or that there is none. A process that uses one page needs four small tables, 16 KiB. One that uses 1 GiB needs 515 of them, about 2 MiB, which is a fifth of one percent of its memory.

The tree has a price, and here it is. Step through the translation of one address:

The 48 bits are cut into four groups of 9 and one of 12. Each group of 9 picks one of the 512 entries in a table, and that entry leads to the next table. The fourth entry gives the frame, and the last 12 bits are the offset. That is four reads of memory before the one read the program asked for. The CPU does this walk by itself, without the kernel, but a machine that paid for it on every access would run at a fraction of its speed.

A cache of translations

So the CPU keeps the translations it has just worked out. The slider sets how many it can keep, and the choice below it changes how the program moves through memory:

This small cache is the TLB, short for translation lookaside buffer. A program that reads memory in order needs a walk only when it enters a new page, so 15 translations in 16 are found in the cache. A program that jumps about among 16 pages, with room for 4 translations, misses most of the time. A PC chip of about 2015 kept 64 translations in a first cache and 1,536 in a second, enough to cover 256 KiB and 6 MiB of memory. Each one is marked with the process it belongs to, so a switch among a few processes does not have to empty the cache.

Pages have cured the holes. One limit is left from the last section, and pages have not touched it: every page still needs a frame. All the programs together cannot be larger than memory, and each must be loaded in full before it can start.

10. More memory than there is

The present bit came in as a way of saying "this page does not exist". It can say something more useful: "not here yet". A fault enters the kernel, and nothing obliges the kernel to end the program. It can put the matter right and let the program try again. Step through a store by sum into a page that has no frame:

sum stores to address 37, in page 2, which is marked not present. The CPU cannot carry the instruction out, so it enters the kernel and hands over the address.

The kernel keeps, for every process, a list of the regions of addresses that the process is entitled to use. The list is drawn up when the program starts, from what its file says it needs, and it grows when the program asks the kernel for more memory with a system call. Address 37 lies in one of the regions. So the kernel takes a free frame, fills it with zeros, writes its number into the page table, sets the present bit and returns to the very same instruction, which now succeeds. sum cannot tell that anything happened.

This is a page fault. The last step shows the other outcome: an address that lies in none of the regions, which is the segmentation fault of the last section.

Nothing until it is touched

With this, a program can start with no memory at all. The next one has 8 pages: 5 of instructions, which lie in its file on the disk, and 3 of data, which start out as zeros. Tap a page to touch it, or let the program run:

The very first instruction faults, and the kernel fetches its page from the program's file. An ordinary run touches 4 of the 8 pages. The others, most of them instructions for things that did not go wrong this time, are never loaded and never cost a frame. A page of fresh data arrives at once, and a page from the file after a wait for the disk.

On a real machine a fault that needs no disk costs around a microsecond. One that has to read a hard disk costs ten milliseconds or more, and one that reads a flash drive about 150 µs. The Atlas computer worked this way in 1962, fetching pages from a magnetic drum when they were first needed. Until then programmers had planned by hand which parts of a large program would be in memory at each moment.

More pages than frames

The same mechanism lets the programs together be larger than memory. Our four processes want 17 pages between them, and there are 12 frames. Change the number of frames:

When no frame is free, the kernel picks a page that has not been used lately, writes it to a part of the disk called swap, and gives its frame away. If the owner touches that page again, the page fault brings it back, and the owner waits 8 ticks for the disk. With 12 frames this happens every ten ticks or so. With 6 only a quarter of the ticks do a program's work, and the rest go on waiting for pages and on the kernel.

How does the kernel know which pages have been used lately? The CPU sets a bit in the page's entry whenever the page is used, and the kernel clears those bits as it goes round. A page whose bit is still clear when the kernel comes round again has not been touched in the meantime.

The choice of page matters more than you might expect. Here are twelve accesses to five pages, handled by three rules. Step through them, and then change the number of frames:

With 3 frames, "oldest arrival first" faults 9 times, "least recently used" 10 times, and the best possible rule, which would have to know the future, 7 times. Now give each rule a fourth frame. Least recently used improves to 8 faults. Oldest-first gets worse, with 10: more memory, and more faults.

This sequence is a famous example from 1969. Least recently used can never behave like that, because the pages it keeps in four frames always include the ones it would keep in three. Real kernels approximate it with the "used" bit, on the reasoning that a page used a moment ago is likely to be wanted again soon.

Too much of a good thing

If programs larger than memory can run, why not run more and more of them? Each process in the next figure needs 3 pages at a time, works for a few ticks and then waits a while for its user, as most programs do. There are 12 frames. Add processes:

Up to four processes everything fits, and each one adds to the work done. Add a fifth, and every process keeps losing pages it is about to need. They spend their time blocked on the disk, the CPU stands idle, and the work done falls to a fifth of what four processes managed. This is thrashing, and the paging systems of the 1960s all ran into it. (The curve you see is this toy's own, not a measurement.)

The cure found then was to let a process run only if the pages it has been using lately fit in memory. Linux is more relaxed. It lets programs reserve more memory than exists, since most never use all they ask for, and when memory really runs out it ends one of them. Phones end apps that are in the background.

A copy for almost nothing

One more thing the writable bit makes possible is copying a whole process without copying its memory. (Why anybody would want a copy of a process is the subject of the next section.) Step through how it is done:

The copy gets a page table of its own that points at the same frames, and every shared page is marked read-only in both tables. Reading costs nothing. The first store by either process faults, and the kernel then copies that one page of 16 cells and gives the writer its own. This is copy-on-write. On a real machine a process holding 6.9 GB was copied this way in 62 ms, because only its page tables had to be duplicated.

So a process can be made cheaply. Which brings up a question I have dodged since section 5, where our processes were simply there when the story began. Who makes them?

11. Where processes come from

On a machine that people share, programs start and stop all day long. So the kernel needs a way to be asked for a new process, and the one doing the asking will be another process, the one a person is typing commands into. First let's take stock of what a process has become. Step through the fields of one row of the process table:

Each of the last few sections left a field behind: the state and the saved registers from section 5, the page table from section 9. Two fields are waiting for sections still to come, the open files and the user. And two are new: a number that names the process, its process ID or PID, and the PID of the process that made it. That row is everything the kernel knows about a running program. In Linux the record runs to several kilobytes.

fork

Unix, which was begun in 1969 on a small computer at Bell Labs, makes a new process in a peculiar way: it copies the process that asks. The system call is fork. Step through process 7 calling it:

The kernel takes a free row and the next free PID, 12. It copies the caller's page table, which costs far less than copying the pages would: the pages themselves are shared, copy-on-write, as at the end of the last section. It copies the saved registers, program counter included, and notes 7 as the origin of the new row. Then it makes the one difference between the two. In the caller, the parent, the call returns 12. In the copy, the child, it returns 0.

So one call returns twice, in two processes, to the same next line of the program, and the test if (pid == 0) sends them different ways. There is no magic in this. The two processes resume from two copies of the same saved registers, which differ in one value.

Fork did not go into Unix for its elegance. The call was borrowed from an earlier time-sharing system at Berkeley, and Dennis Ritchie recalled that on their first machine it "required precisely 27 lines of assembly code".

exec

A copy of the parent is rarely what was wanted. The second call, exec, turns the copy into something else:

exec does not make a process. It empties the address space of the process that calls it and sets it up again from a program file: regions for the program's instructions and data, a fresh stack, the scratch space for its function calls, with the program's arguments on it, and the program counter at the first instruction. Nothing is loaded yet, because the pages will arrive through page faults, as in the last section. The row keeps its PID, its parent and its open files.

So starting a program takes two steps: fork a copy, and let the copy exec. It looks roundabout, and it has its critics. But the gap between the two steps is useful. In it the child is still running the parent's code and can rearrange its own affairs before it becomes the new program. We will see the use of that in section 14. Windows does it in a single call, which takes ten parameters.

exit and wait

Processes also end. Press the buttons in different orders:

When a process calls exit, the kernel frees its memory and keeps its row. The row holds one number, the exit status, by which the process says how things went. It stays until the parent collects that number with the call wait. A process in this state, ended but not yet collected, is called a zombie. It takes up a row and nothing else, and it cannot be ended a second time.

If the parent ends first, the child is handed to process 1, the first process on the machine and the ancestor of every ordinary one, which collects whatever is left to it.

The program that starts programs

The program that reads your commands in a terminal (today usually a window that plays the part of one) is called a shell, and with these three calls we can read its heart. Choose a command and press Enter:

The loop is ten lines long. Read a line. Fork. The child execs the program named on the line, and the parent waits for it. Then the shell prints its prompt again. The command cd, which changes the current directory (one more field of a process's row, which I left out above), is handled by the shell itself, without a fork, and it has to be. Run it as a separate program, and the child changes its own directory and exits, leaving the shell where it was.

Unix's authors met exactly this soon after they added fork. Ritchie called it the most memorable of their surprises: the command for changing directory "had stopped working".

Too many

A process table has a last row. Here is a program whose only instruction is "fork, and again":

The rows double with every tick until the table is full. After that nobody can start anything, including the command that would end the offenders: the shell's own fork fails with "Resource temporarily unavailable". Limit the rows that one person's programs may hold, and the flood stops at the limit, with room left for someone to act. Linux allows 32,768 process IDs unless told otherwise, and about four million at most.

Everything in this section lives in memory: the rows, the pages, the results. Switch the machine off and all of it is gone. Meanwhile I have been saying that sum reads its list "from a tape" and that exec reads a program "from a file". It is time to look at where things are kept.

12. Names on a disk

A disk keeps what is written on it when the power goes off. What it offers the kernel is very plain. Tap a block to read it, and try eight blocks in a row against eight that are scattered:

A disk is a row of numbered blocks, and it can do two things: read block n and write block n. A spinning disk keeps its blocks in circular tracks on a turning platter, and an arm has to travel to the right track and wait for the block to come round.

On a common drive that turns 7,200 times a minute, a block somewhere else on the disk takes about 13 ms to reach, which makes some 76 scattered reads a second. Blocks in a row pass under the arm one after another, hundreds of times faster. (The toy disk in the figure shows the same effect on a much smaller scale.) A flash drive has no arm, and reads any block in about a tenth of a millisecond.

The first hard disk on sale, IBM's of 1956, held 5 million characters on fifty platters two feet across. What was new about it was that it could reach any record in under a second. A tape has to be wound to the place.

Which blocks are mine

People and programs do not want numbered blocks. They want named things that can grow. From here on our list is such a thing, a file on the disk, and the first question is how to record which blocks a file occupies. The plainest answer is a run of neighbouring blocks, noted as a first block and a length:

File A cannot grow, because the block after it belongs to B. And once B and D are deleted, four blocks are free in two places, and a file of four blocks does not fit. These are the holes of section 8 again, on a disk.

The next idea is a chain. Each block of a file names the block that follows it. Pick a block of the file to read:

Now a file can grow into any free block. But to reach block 6 the disk has to read blocks 0 to 5 first, seven reads for one block. The repair is to keep all the links together in one table, which is stored on the disk and held in memory while the disk is in use, so that following them costs no disk reads at all. This is the "file allocation table" that gives the FAT format of memory cards its name. The format notes a file's size in 4 bytes, which is why no file on such a card can reach 4 GiB.

The inode

Unix took a third way: one small record per file that lists the file's blocks itself. The record is called an inode. Use the slider to make the file larger:

An inode says who owns the file, what may be done with it, how large it is and when it was changed, and, in the layout Linux used for many years, it has fifteen slots for block numbers. The first twelve point straight at blocks of data. With blocks of 4 KiB that covers 48 KiB, and since most files are smaller, most files are reached in a single step.

The thirteenth slot points at a block that is full of block numbers, 1,024 of them, which adds 4 MiB. The fourteenth points at a block of such blocks and adds 4 GiB, and the fifteenth goes one level further and adds 4 TiB. Even the last block of an enormous file is only three extra reads away, and small files pay nothing for that.

(Ext4, the format many Linux systems use for their disks, notes runs of blocks instead, "a thousand blocks starting at this one", and four such notes fit in the inode.)

Names

One thing an inode does not hold is the file's name. Names are kept in a directory, which is itself a file whose contents are pairs: a name, and the number of an inode. A path such as /home/ana/list.txt is followed one name at a time. Step through it on our toy disk of 64 blocks:

The toy disk has a fixed layout: first a block that describes the disk as a whole, then two maps with one bit for every inode and for every block, saying which are in use, then the inodes, then the blocks of data.

The kernel reads the inode of /, the directory everything hangs from, and then that directory's block, where it finds "home" and the number 4. It reads inode 4 and its block, and finds "ana" and 5. It reads inode 5 and its block, and finds "list.txt" and 8. Inode 8 says that the file is one block long and that the block is number 13. That makes seven reads to find the file, and the eighth fetches the list: two reads for each name on the way, and one more.

A name, then, is only an entry in a directory. Give the file a second one, and then take names away:

A second name is a second entry with the same inode number. Neither is the "real" one, and the inode keeps count of how many it has. Removing a name removes one entry and lowers the count. Only when the count reaches zero are the inode and its blocks marked free, and even then nothing erases the bytes in them. The system call that does this is not called "delete". It is called unlink.

An open file

Following a path for every read would be absurd, so a program opens a file once and keeps a handle to it. Step through a few calls:

open follows the path, makes an entry in the kernel's table of open files, holding a position in the file and a pointer to the inode, and gives the program a small number, a file descriptor. The descriptor is simply a place in a table that belongs to the process. Places 0, 1 and 2 are taken before a program starts, here by the terminal, and section 14 will say why. Each read moves the position along. After a fork the child's descriptor leads to the same entry, so parent and child share one position. A separate open of the same file gets a position of its own.

The whole arrangement on the disk, with its inodes, directories and maps of what is free, is a file system.

It works, and it is slow. Eight reads at 13 ms each come to a tenth of a second, to fetch a small file whose blocks have not changed since yesterday.

13. Surviving a power cut

The remedy for a slow disk is one you know from the CPU page: keep a copy of what was fetched somewhere fast. Memory is about a hundred thousand times faster than a spinning disk, so the kernel keeps every block it reads in a spare frame. The figure starts with a first read of the list. Read it again, and then let a program ask for memory:

The first read waits 8 ticks for the disk. The second is answered from memory in none. This is the page cache, and it lives in whatever frames the programs are not using. The moment a program needs those frames the cached blocks simply vanish, because the disk still has them. That is why a Linux machine that has been running for a while reports hardly any free memory. It is full of cache, all of which is handed back on demand.

The inodes and directories on the way to a file are cached in the same way, so the eight reads of the last section shrink to none the second time.

Writing is harder

The cache works for writing too, and there it has a price. Watch the editor save its notes every few seconds, and then pull the plug:

A save changes the block in the cache and returns at once. The block in memory now differs from the one on the disk, and is said to be dirty. Every 5 seconds a part of the kernel looks through the cache and writes out the blocks that have been dirty for 30 seconds. (These are the settings Linux starts with.) So work the editor was told had been saved can exist in memory alone for half a minute, and a power cut takes it.

A program that cannot afford this makes one more system call, fsync, which means "do not come back until this is on the disk". Switch it on, and nothing is lost, but every save now waits for the disk: 17 to 25 ms on a spinning one, in one set of measurements.

Three writes

Losing the last half-minute of work is bearable. What is worse is that the plug can be pulled in the middle of one change. To add a single block to the editor's file, the kernel has to change three blocks on the disk. Use the switches to say which of the three were written before the power went:

The three are the new block of data, the file's inode, which gains a block number and a larger size, and the map that says which blocks are in use. The disk writes them one at a time. If only the inode got there, the file now includes a block that still holds somebody's old bytes, and the map calls that block free, so it will be given to another file as well. If only the map got there, a block is marked as used that no file owns, and it is lost until somebody checks the whole disk. Of the eight possibilities, five leave some such mess.

Checking everything

The first remedy was to check the whole disk after every crash. Choose a size of disk and run the check:

The checker trusts the inodes. It reads every one of them, rebuilds the map from what they say and puts right whatever disagrees. It cannot spot a file that points at old bytes, since nothing about that looks wrong. And the time it needs follows the size of the disk, not the three blocks that were in flight. On real disks the reports run from many minutes to hours, and to two days for disks of several terabytes.

Write it down first

The remedy in use today is older than computers: before doing something that must not be left half done, write down what you are about to do. Step through one append, and choose where the power fails:

A strip of the disk is set apart as a journal. Before touching the file's own blocks, the kernel writes copies of the three changed blocks into the journal. Then it writes one last small block after them, the commit, which a disk writes entirely or not at all. Only then do the three blocks go to their real places. Such a group of changes that must happen together is a transaction.

If the power fails before the commit, the next start finds an entry without its commit and ignores it, and the file is as it was. If it fails after, the next start finds a complete entry and carries it out again, which does no harm however often it is done. The file is the old one or the new one and never a mixture, and the restart reads only the journal, however large the disk.

The cost is that everything is written twice. So Linux's usual setting journals only the inode and the map, and writes the data block to its place before the commit. Windows has had a journal of this kind since 1993 and Linux since 2001.

Never overwrite

The newer answer is the copy-on-write of section 10, applied to a disk: never overwrite a block that is in use. Step through the same append:

The changed data goes into a free block. Then a new copy of the inode that points at it is written into another free block, then a new copy of the block that records where that inode is, and so on up to the top. (A file system of this kind keeps nothing in a fixed place, as ours kept its inodes.) Last of all a single pointer is switched from the old top to the new one.

Until that one write, the old version of everything is still complete on the disk, and a power cut leaves it so. If the old top is kept instead of freed, it is a snapshot of the whole disk as it was. The file system of Apple's devices since 2017 works like this, and so do ZFS and Btrfs.

So much for the disk. But the disk is one device, and a machine has dozens of kinds, each with its own cells and its own habits.

14. Everything looks like a file

The last thing sum does is print its total, and it does it with one line: write(1, "31\n", 3), "write these three bytes to descriptor 1". Where that is, the line does not say. Choose what descriptor 1 points to:

Descriptor 1 leads to an entry for an open file, and every such entry carries a table of functions: how to write to this thing, how to read from it, how to close it. If the entry stands for the screen, the functions belong to the code that works the terminal. If it stands for a file on the disk, they belong to the file system. If it stands for a pipe, which we will come to in a moment, they put the bytes in a buffer. If it stands for the file called /dev/null, they throw the bytes away.

The line in sum is the same every time, and sum cannot tell the difference.

By convention descriptor 0 is a program's standard input and descriptor 1 its standard output, with 2 for error messages. A well-behaved program reads from 0 and writes to 1, and leaves it to whoever started it to decide what those are. Unix carried the idea through to devices: each has a name in the directory /dev and is opened, read and written like a file.

Drivers

For a device, that table of functions, together with the handler for the device's interrupts, is called a driver. Step through a new printer being plugged in:

Nothing can use the printer until its driver, written by people who know that printer, has been linked into the running kernel. Then a name for it appears in /dev, and any program can open that name and write to it with the calls it already knows.

The last step shows the price. On Linux a driver runs in kernel mode, where nothing is protected from it, so one wrong store by a driver halts the machine and every program on it. And drivers are about half of a kernel. In 2007 they made up 52% of Linux's lines, and a study of 2001 found that driver code had up to three to seven times the rate of errors of the rest.

Pipes

One more kind of thing can sit behind a descriptor, and it belongs to no device. Set how fast one process writes and another reads:

A pipe is a buffer inside the kernel with a descriptor at each end, one for writing and one for reading. If the writer is faster, the buffer fills, and the writer is blocked, in the sense of section 5, until the reader has made room. If the reader is faster, it is the reader that is blocked. When the writer closes its end, the reader takes what is left and is then told that the data has ended. Neither process knows about the other. Each just writes to a descriptor or reads from one.

The idea is older than Unix. In 1964 Doug McIlroy wrote that there should be ways of "connecting programs like garden hose". Ken Thompson added pipes to Unix in a single night, in 1972 or early 1973. On Linux a pipe holds 65,536 bytes.

The shell's wiring

All that is left is for somebody to connect the ends, and that somebody is the shell. Step through what it does with the command line cat list.txt | sum, where cat is a program that copies a file to its standard output:

The shell makes a pipe and forks twice. In the gap between fork and exec, the gap I promised a use for in section 11, the first child makes its descriptor 1 a copy of the pipe's writing end, and the second child makes its descriptor 0 a copy of the reading end. Each then execs its program. cat writes to its standard output as it always does, and sum reads its standard input. Neither contains a word about pipes.

After that the shell only waits. It does not carry the data, and the two programs run at the same time. The command line sum < list.txt > total.txt is the same trick played with two files.

One keystroke

We can now follow a single keystroke through almost everything on this page so far. primes is running in a terminal, and you press Ctrl-C to stop it:

The keyboard interrupts (section 4), and the handler receives the byte 3. The kernel's terminal code recognises 3 as the interrupt character, so it does not pass it on as input. Instead it sends primes a signal. A signal is a small numbered message from the kernel to a process, saying that something has happened, and number 2 means "interrupted from the keyboard". Sending it is no more than setting a mark, "signal 2 pending", in the row of primes in the process table.

The next time the kernel is about to return to primes in user mode, which is at the end of its time slice at the latest (section 6), it sees the mark. A process can tell the kernel in advance which of its functions to run when a given signal arrives. primes has not, and for most signals the kernel then ends the process. The shell, blocked in wait (section 11), wakes up, learns that its child was ended by signal 2 and prints its prompt. The shell itself did nothing to stop the program.

One thing has not changed since section 1. Each of our programs still runs on a single core, however many the machine has.

15. Two cores, one total

Suppose sum has read its whole list into its own memory, and the machine has two cores. Adding the eight numbers takes 16 ticks on one core while the other stands idle. A second process would not help much, since it would have an address space and a total of its own. What is wanted is a second line of execution inside the same process. Switch from one to two:

Such a line of execution is a thread. It has registers, a program counter and a stack of its own, and it shares everything else with the other threads of its process: the address space, and so the list, and the open files. With two threads, one on each core, the first adds the first four numbers in a register of its own and gets 9, the second adds the other four and gets 22, and the two results are added at the end: 31 after 9 ticks where it took 16.

You have used threads in your programming language. To the kernel a thread is the thing that gets scheduled, and on Linux threads and processes are made by one and the same system call, with flags that say what the newcomer shares with its maker. (Every process in sections 5 to 7 had exactly one thread, so there the difference did not show.)

One total

That version was careful: each thread kept a subtotal to itself. The obvious way to write it is for both threads to add straight into the one total in memory. But total += x is three instructions: load the total into a register, add the number, store the register back. Here you run the machine by hand. Each button lets one thread carry out its next instruction (until you press one, the figure plays an order of its own):

Let one thread finish before the other starts, and the total is 31. Now let thread 1 load the total, which is 0, and then let thread 2 load it too. Both add, and both store: one writes 3 and the other 5. An addition has vanished, although each thread did exactly what it was written to do. A mistake that depends on the order in which things happen to occur is a race. The worst order leaves a total of 6, and in all, 25 different totals are possible.

How often does it go wrong in practice? Here the two threads run the whole sum again and again:

On one core nearly every run gives 31, because a switch has to fall exactly between a load and its store. On two cores the three steps overlap all the time, and wrong totals turn up often, and differently on each run. In a real measurement, two threads that each added 1 ten million times produced 19,345,221 on one run and 19,221,041 on the next. This is why such mistakes survive testing: the program is right most of the time.

A lock

The cure is to let only one thread at a time be between its load and its store. That stretch of the program is a critical section, and it is guarded by one more cell of memory, a lock (also called a mutex), which holds 0 when it is free and 1 when it is taken. Step through both threads arriving at once:

The first step shows the obvious attempt failing. To read the lock, see a 0 and then write a 1 takes two instructions, and both threads can read the 0 before either writes: the same race, moved to another cell. What rescues us is a special instruction, SWAP in the figure, that writes a 1 into the cell and hands back what was there before, in a single step that no other core can get into the middle of. A step like that is called atomic.

The thread that gets back a 0 holds the lock. The thread that gets back a 1 knows it was taken, and tries again. Thread 1 does its three instructions and puts a 0 back, and no addition can be lost any more. Every CPU has an instruction, or a pair of instructions, of this kind, and every lock in every program you have written rests on it.

Two ways to wait

What should a thread do while the lock is taken? There are two answers. The slider sets how long the holder keeps the lock:

On the left the waiting thread tries again in a loop. A lock used this way is a spinlock. It costs nothing if the lock comes free at once, and it burns a whole core for as long as the lock is held. On the right the thread asks the kernel to block it. Its core goes to primes meanwhile, at the price of two entries into the kernel, one to be blocked and one to be woken. For a lock held one tick, trying again is cheaper. For a long hold, blocking is.
