The locks of Linux combine the two. Taking a free lock is one atomic instruction and no system call, and taking and releasing one costs about 25 ns, by one widely quoted list of such figures. The kernel is called only when the lock turns out to be taken.

Two locks

Locks bring a failure of their own. Here are two of them, A and B, and two threads that each need both. Step the threads yourself:

Thread 1 takes A and then asks for B. Thread 2 takes B and then asks for A. Let each take its first lock, and both are blocked for ever, each waiting for what the other holds. This is a deadlock. Neither thread is wrong when looked at alone. Make both take A first, and whatever you do, one of them simply waits its turn. "Always take locks in the same order" is the rule that programs with more than one lock live by.

A lock on Mars

The last failure needs a scheduler with priorities, as in section 7, and it happened a long way from home. Step through it:

In July 1997, a few days into its mission, the Mars Pathfinder lander began resetting its computer. (Its system called its threads tasks.) A low-priority task that gathered weather data held a lock. A high-priority task needed that lock and was blocked, which should have lasted a moment.

But tasks of medium priority, which needed no lock at all, outranked the low one and kept it off the CPU. So it could not release the lock, the high task waited past its deadline, and the task at the very top, which ran the lander's data bus, found the high task unfinished and reset the whole computer. This is priority inversion.

The fix lets the holder of a lock borrow the priority of whoever is waiting for it. The engineers reproduced the fault on a copy of the lander on Earth in under 18 hours, and sent the change to Mars.

Threads share a process. The next question is how people share a machine.

16. Whose file is it

Time sharing put many people on one machine, with all their files on one disk. Ben can type the path of Ana's list as easily as she can. But the kernel is the only way to a file, as we saw in section 3, so the kernel can decide. It needs to know two things: who is asking, and what the file allows.

A word first. A user from here on is a person's account on the machine. That has nothing to do with the "user" in "user mode", which is just the mode every program runs in. Each user has a number, the user ID, and every process carries the user ID of whoever started it, handed down from parent to child at each fork. Every inode holds the user ID of the file's owner, the ID of a group of users, and nine permission bits. Choose who is asking and for what:

The nine bits are three sets of three: read, write and run, written r, w and x, once for the owner, once for the members of the file's group, and once for everybody else. The kernel picks exactly one of the three sets: the owner's if the process belongs to the owner, otherwise the group's if it belongs to a member, otherwise the last. With rw-r----- on the list, Ana can read and write it, Ben, who is in the group, can read it, and Dan can do nothing.

There is no falling through from one set to the next. With the odd setting ---rwxrwx Ana, who owns the file, is refused, while everybody else is allowed. One user ID is exempt from nearly all of it: 0, the administrator, known as root. (Even root can run only a file that has an x bit set somewhere.)

Borrowing root

This simple rule soon needs an exception. The file of passwords can be written by root alone. So how does Ben change his own password? Step through it:

Ben's editor cannot open the file. But the program that changes passwords belongs to root and carries one extra bit, called setuid. When Ben runs it, exec sees the bit and makes the process act as the owner of the program file, which is root, for as long as that program runs. The program is trusted to do one narrow thing: it checks that Ben is changing Ben's line and nobody else's.

Dennis Ritchie applied for a patent on this bit in 1973. It is elegant, and it is dangerous, because any mistake in such a program is a mistake made as root.

A program you run is you

The rule has a larger hole. Ana has downloaded a game. Start it:

The check asks which user a process belongs to. It never asks which program it is. The game runs as Ana, so when it opens her notes the kernel finds the owner asking, and allows it. The game then sends the notes out through the network, and nothing we have built objects.

The repair is to run the game in a sandbox. A sandbox gives a program an identity and a list of rights of its own. Here the game gets its own user ID, as every app on an Android phone does, and it runs behind a filter that lists the system calls it may make. Now opening the notes is refused by the nine bits, and reaching the network is refused by the filter. Phones and browsers do some version of this today.

All of root, or one right

Root is the opposite problem: too much power in one place. A service, which is a program that runs in the background and answers requests from the network, needs one privileged thing, such as the right to listen at a network address reserved for the system, and the old way to give it that one thing was to run it as root. Break into it:

Whoever finds a flaw in a service that runs as root holds the whole machine. On 2 November 1988 a program now called the Morris worm spread through just such flaws in the network services of Unix machines. How many machines it reached is disputed: the usual figure of 6,000 is a tenth of somebody's guess at the size of the network, and another count came to about 2,000.

Linux now splits root's power into 41 separate rights. Give the service only the one it needs, and an intruder gets that one and no more.

Every break-in needs a flaw to get in through, and most such flaws are of one kind: mistakes in handling memory, which the language C does nothing to prevent. Microsoft has said that about 70% of the security flaws it repairs each year are of this kind, and the Chrome browser's team reports the same share of its serious ones. So new code is moving to languages that rule such mistakes out. Linux has accepted code in Rust since December 2022.

A protection that leaked

One protection built on this page has failed outright. In section 9 the kernel's pages sat in every process's page table, guarded only by the user bit. The figure shows the repair and what it costs. The failure itself I can only describe:

In January 2018 it became known that many CPUs which run ahead on guesses, Intel's above all, could be made to read those pages before the check on the bit took effect, and to leak what they read. (Running ahead on guesses is the subject of the CPU page's last sections.) The flaw was named Meltdown. The repair gives every process a second page table without the kernel's pages in it, and switches tables on every entry to the kernel and every return. Each switch takes time, and on older CPUs it also empties the cache of translations.

What that costs depends on how often a program enters the kernel. Below 10,000 system calls a second on each core the loss was put at under half a percent. At 210,000 a second a quarter of the program's speed was measured to be gone.

We have now explained every part of a running system. We have said nothing about how it gets running.

17. From the power button

When the power comes on, memory holds nothing of use. The kernel is a file on the disk, reading a file takes a file system, and the file system is part of the kernel. Something has to load the program that loads programs. The old picture for this is pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps, which is where the word boot comes from. Step through our machine starting:

The answer is a chain of loaders, each just able to find and start the next, larger one. The CPU is built to begin at a fixed address, in a chip that keeps its contents without power. The program in that chip is the firmware. It checks the memory, finds the disk, copies one block from it into memory and jumps there. That block holds the boot loader, which knows just enough about the file system to find the kernel's file, load it, many times its own size, and jump again.

The kernel then sets itself up, in an order we will come to, and builds the row for process 1 by hand, there being nobody yet to fork from. Process 1 runs a program traditionally called init, which forks and execs everything else, down to your shell.

On PCs with a hard disk and the older kind of firmware, known as the BIOS, that first block was 512 bytes long, of which 446 were program. Before there were such chips, the first loader was entered by hand, on a row of switches. (A real disk keeps its first blocks free for the loader, in front of the file system. Our toy disk of section 12 did not, so here the loader simply takes block 0.)

Trusting the chain

Whatever runs before the kernel runs with none of this page's protections around it: no modes that mean anything, no fences, no permission bits. Choose a stage that somebody has tampered with, and power on:

An altered loader or kernel owns the machine before any defence exists, and decides what every later stage will be. Switch the checking off to see it happen.

So today each stage checks a signature on the next before jumping to it. A signature is a number worked out from a program's bytes, which only the program's maker could have produced and which anyone can check against the maker's key. The chain begins from a key kept in the firmware, which on phones is fixed in the chip, and an altered stage is never run. PCs do this through UEFI, the firmware standard that replaced the BIOS, and machines sold with Windows have had to since 2012. iPhones and Android phones do it too.

The first seconds

The kernel's own start retraces this page. Step through the order in which Linux brings up its parts:

It begins on one core, with interrupts off. First come the rows of the interrupt table that deal with faults, so that from here on the kernel's own mistakes are caught. Then memory, and then the scheduler and the process table, which need memory. Then the rows for devices, and the timer. Only now are interrupts switched on, since any earlier one would have arrived with no handler to receive it. After that come the beginnings of process 1, the other cores, the drivers, the file system on the disk, and finally init. Each part is built from the parts before it, in nearly the order we built them.

Where the time goes

The top bar shows the start of one laptop, as measured by its owner in 2022. Below it are eight services, the background programs such as the network and the clock that process 1 has to start. Flip the switch:

On that laptop the firmware took 8.8 seconds and the boot loader 3.4. The kernel needed half a second, and another half for a small first file system held in memory, which carries the drivers needed to reach the real disk. The login screen was up 2.4 seconds after that, though two slow services kept this last stage going for 19 seconds. The kernel is the quick part.

The services are where the time can be won. One after another, the eight in this toy take 17 seconds. Started side by side, each as soon as the ones it depends on are up, they take 8, and that is how process 1 works on most Linux systems today.

So a machine starts, and runs one kernel. That holds however large the machine is, and however little of it any one program needs.

18. Machines inside machines

One kernel per machine is often the wrong number. A computing centre today rents out parts of its machines to strangers. Each of them wants a whole machine, with an operating system of their own choosing, and none of them should be able to touch the others.

What would it take to run an entire kernel as an ordinary program? A kernel expects to be in kernel mode. The trick is not to give it that. Step through a system call inside such a setup:

The visiting system is called the guest, and its kernel runs in user mode. Every privileged instruction the guest's kernel tries is refused and enters the real kernel, which in this role is called a hypervisor. For the guest the hypervisor keeps a pretend machine: a mode bit, an interrupt table, a tape that is really a file. It carries out the refused instruction on the pretend machine and lets the guest continue. The guest's kernel never finds out that it is not in charge.

A system run in this way is a virtual machine, and the real machine under it is the host. IBM ran systems like this from 1967. It works on one condition: every instruction that behaves differently in user mode has to be refused there, so that the hypervisor gets to hear of it.

The PC did not qualify

On the CPUs of PCs, seventeen instructions, by one count, broke that condition. The slider sets how often a guest has to hand over to the hypervisor:

The left side shows one of the seventeen, the instruction a kernel uses to restore whether interrupts are on. In user mode it quietly did nothing. It was not refused, so the hypervisor was never told, and the guest went on believing something false about its own machine. In 1999 a product for PCs got round this by rewriting the guest kernel's code as it ran, which was slow for code that entered the kernel often.

In 2005 and 2006 Intel and AMD built the remedy into the CPU: a guest mode with a user mode and a kernel mode of its own, which is left for the hypervisor only on chosen events. Each such round trip cost 3,963 ticks of the CPU's clock on the first chips and 784 by 2011. At 100,000 round trips a second that is 13% of a core running at 3 GHz in the first case and under 3% in the second.

Memory needs the same treatment. The guest's kernel keeps page tables for its processes, but what it takes for frames of memory are themselves pages handed to it by the host. Step through one translation:

There are now two sets of page tables. The guest's turn a program's address into what the guest believes is a memory address, and the hypervisor's turn that into a real one. The CPU walks both. Each of the guest's four tables lies at a believed address, which costs four reads to find and one to read, and the final address costs four more: up to 24 reads where there were 4. The TLB of section 9 is what makes this bearable, because it remembers the end result.

With all this in hardware, computing inside a virtual machine costs little. One comparison in 2014 measured a loss of 2% on pure arithmetic, once the virtual machine had been tuned. The costs that remain are in work that leans on memory and in input and output: the same study found 18% on a compression job, where the double walk is the suspect, and network round trips that took 80% longer.

Containers

The other answer is not to bring a second kernel at all. Compare the two, and press the buttons:

A container is a group of ordinary processes on the host's own kernel, with their view of the system narrowed. A system call made inside a virtual machine lands in that machine's own kernel. One made inside a container lands in the kernel that everybody shares. That makes containers light. In the 2014 comparison one started in under a second where a virtual machine took 11, and it carries no kernel of its own in memory.

It also makes the wall thinner. A flaw in the shared kernel, with nearly 400 system calls open to every tenant, is everybody's flaw. So people have built virtual machines that are nearly as light: one design of 2018 starts a small one in 125 ms with about 3 MB of overhead, where the classic program for running virtual machines needs 131 MB.

What is the narrowed view made of? Flip the three switches:

It is made of separate tables of names, called namespaces. Given its own table of process IDs, a program believes that it is process 1 and sees only its own children, while the host sees it as process 4012 among all the rest. Given its own table of attached file systems and its own network table, it sees its own files under / and its own addresses. (A machine can hold several file systems, each attached at some directory, and that table says which is where.) Nothing else has changed. For these processes the kernel simply looks names up in different tables.

Hiding names does not stop a process from taking everything, though. Here two containers share the machine's frames, and one of them is greedy:

With no limit the greedy program takes every free frame, and its neighbours' pages are pushed out to the disk, with the waits of section 10. With a limit it is ended, in this toy, the moment its group reaches its ceiling, and the neighbours never notice. (A real kernel first tries to take memory back from the group.) The mechanism is a control group: the kernel counts the memory, the CPU time and the number of processes each group uses, and enforces a ceiling on each.

Namespaces, control groups and a bundle of files to run: that is all a container is. The pieces entered Linux between 2002 and 2013, and Docker made a convenient package of them in 2013.

That was the last part to add. What is left is to see all of them at work together.

19. Today's systems

Everything on this page is at work in the machine you are reading it on. In section 14 we followed Ctrl-C through the kernel. Here is the whole journey of an ordinary key, in a terminal window on a Linux desktop, from the switch under the key to the letter on the screen:

The keyboard has a small computer of its own, which notices the switch close and holds a report until the USB controller collects it. The controller interrupts (section 4). A driver (section 14) turns the report into a key event and queues it on a file in /dev. The program that draws the windows was blocked reading that file (section 5). It is woken, the scheduler runs it (section 7), and it reads the event with a system call (section 3).

That program passes the key to the terminal window, through a channel much like a pipe (section 14). The terminal window writes a byte to the shell, the shell writes the letter back, and the terminal draws it. Then the picture waits for the display's next refresh, which at 60 pictures a second can be up to 16.7 ms away. One letter takes many entries into the kernel and several context switches, between at least three processes.

What does it all add up to? Here are 21 measurements of computers made between 1977 and 2017, from the moment a key starts to move to the moment the screen changes:

An Apple IIe of 1983 answered in 30 ms. It had almost nothing between the key and the screen. Linux desktops of 2016 and 2017 took 90 to 170 ms, close to or beyond the tenth of a second at which a response stops feeling instant. Rank them by their wait, and machines of the early 1980s take the first two places. Every layer on the path of the keypress has a good reason to exist, and every one adds its wait.

Inside or outside

One large question of design has stayed open through all of this: how much should run in kernel mode? Choose a design, then read a file and break a driver:

Linux keeps everything inside: the scheduler, memory, the file systems, the network code and nearly every driver. Such a kernel is called a monolithic kernel. A read is one entry into it, and one faulty driver can stop everything, as we saw in section 14. The other design, the microkernel, keeps only address spaces, scheduling and the passing of messages inside. File systems, network code and drivers become ordinary processes. In this figure the same read now passes between user mode and kernel mode eight times where it passed twice, and a driver that fails is restarted like any other program.

In 1992 Andrew Tanenbaum, the author of the teaching system MINIX, called the new Linux kernel "a giant step back into the 1970s". Speed decided the matter on desktops and servers: in the early 1990s a message between processes took about 100 µs, and designs twenty times faster came after Linux had appeared. Windows and macOS also keep nearly all of theirs inside.

Microkernels run today where being right matters more than being fast, in the modems of phones and in the security chip of iPhones. One of them, 8,700 lines of C, comes with a proof, checked by machine, that the code does what its specification says.

Two families

Nearly everything that runs today comes from two families. Move the year:

Unix dates from 1969. Through BSD, the version developed at Berkeley from 1977, it lies under macOS and iOS, which are built on it. Linux, announced on 25 August 1991 as "just a hobby", is a new kernel built to the same model. It lies under Android, and it has run every one of the 500 fastest computers in the world since November 2017. The other family begins with Windows NT in 1993.

In one survey of web traffic in October 2026, about 77% of the page views from desktop machines came from Windows, 16% from Macs and 6% from Linux. Among phones, 72% came from Android and 28% from iOS.

And here is how large one of these has grown:

Linux was 10,239 lines in 1991 and 176,250 in 1994. In 2007 it had 8.2 million, 52% of them drivers. In 2020 it had 28 million, and in 2026 about 40 million. By an estimate of 2020, a laptop runs about 2 million of them. The rest are drivers for hardware it does not have and code for kinds of CPU it is not. In one release cycle of 63 days in 2026, a record 3,021 people made 18,765 changes, about twelve an hour.

The fourth program

Let's go back to where we started. This is the machine from the top of the page, still running its three programs. Step forward to uncover what is under them:

The violet ticks between the programs were never mysterious. They are a handful of tables and the code that reads and writes them: an interrupt table, a process table and its queue, a page table for each process, the open files, the inodes and the cache in front of the disk. That code can be entered only through one door, which a program opens with a trap, a device with an interrupt and the CPU itself with a fault. That is the heart of an operating system, its kernel. The other forty million lines are details, and about half of them are drivers.

Further reading

These are the sources I found most useful, in roughly the order of the page.

  • Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau: a free textbook that climbs much the same ladder as this page, with small worked numbers for every scheduler, page table and file system.
  • General Motors/North American Monitor for the IBM 704 Computer, by Robert Patrick: fourteen pages by one of its designers, with the setup timings, the rents and the reasons.
  • John McCarthy's memo on time sharing: three pages, and the complaint about waiting 3 to 36 hours that started it.
  • The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System, by Dennis Ritchie: short and first-hand, on what broke on the first Unix machine and what was added to mend it, fork and pipes included.
  • xv6: a complete small Unix written for teaching. Its shell, fork, wait and pipe are a few hundred lines of readable C.
  • Before Memory Was Virtual, by Peter Denning: the history of paging, thrashing and its cure, by the person who found the cure.
  • The TTY demystified, by Linus Åkesson: a clear account of terminals, Ctrl-C and signals.
  • What really happened on Mars, by Glenn Reeves: the Pathfinder resets, told by the leader of the flight software team.
  • Computer latency: 1977–2017, by Dan Luu: the keypress measurements of the last section, and where the milliseconds go.

Final words

Go back to the browser, the editor and the terminal you had open at the top of the page, each sure that it has the machine to itself.

You can now say how that is arranged. A timer takes the CPU away from each of them many times a second, and a scheduler decides who gets it next. A page table for each one makes the same address mean a different cell of memory. Under every file name there is one long row of numbered blocks, with a journal to keep it whole when the power fails. And between the programs and all of it stands a fourth program, entered through a single door many thousands of times a second.

It was built over seventy years, one repair at a time, each made because something had just gone wrong. I hope that the next time something does, you will have an idea where to look.
